title: European robin
summary: The European robin (Erithacus rubecula): a small songbird, about 14 cm long and 19 g, with an orange face and breast.

layers.basics: This is the robin of British gardens and parks: a plump little bird with an orange-red face and breast, a brown back, a pale belly and thin legs. It stands here, alert, on a boulder. Use the layer buttons to peel it: feathers, skin, muscles, skeleton, organs, air sacs and lungs, nerves. Click any part for its card. Everything is drawn at its real size, so zoom right in.
layers.deeper: A robin is a passerine, a perching bird. Its body is built for flight with very little weight: hollow bones, a big keel on the breastbone to hold the flight muscles, a fused hand, feathers, and a lung that works with air sacs. Its song, its territory and the orange breast that rivals read as a signal are all part of how it lives. The cards link each part to the human structure it matches (a wing is an arm) and to the molecules at the bottom of the scale.
layers.expert: The model is a procedural reconstruction. Overall size and the published feather counts (10 primaries, 9 secondaries including 3 tertials, 12 tail feathers) are used; the proportions of every part and the size and place of every organ are drawn by eye from photographs and anatomical drawings and are approximate. Colours follow the plumage description in the sources. The bird stands still; breathing and the heartbeat are illustrations, not measured movements.

facts: 16 to 22 g; adult average ≈ 19 g (females 19.2 g, males 18.5 g; BTO)
≈ 1 to 2 years; ringing record 8 years 4 months (BTO)

title: How a robin flies
summary: A flying bird gets lift from air flowing over its wings; flapping tilts that force forward to push the bird along.

layers.basics: Lift is a force at right angles to the air flowing past a wing. The wing is shaped and tilted so that the air curves around it and ends up pushed downward, and by the same exchange the wing is pushed up. It is not enough to say that flapping pushes air down: the wing makes lift because air is moving over it, which is why a bird gliding with its wings still held out stays up. In flapping flight the downstroke makes the lift and most of the forward push; on the upstroke the wing is folded a little to cut the cost.
layers.deeper: The muscles that move the wing tilt the lift forward, so part of the force is thrust that beats the drag and raises speed, and the higher speed makes more lift to balance weight. A bird changes the angle of its wing to the air all the time during each beat and as its speed changes. The alula, the small group of feathers at the front of the wrist, helps hold the airflow on the wing at low speed, as when landing. Energy lost to lift-induced drag ends up mainly in vortices shed from the wing tips.
layers.expert: The lift on a wing of area S in air of density ρ at speed v is L = ½ρv²S·C_L, where the lift coefficient C_L rises with the angle of attack up to the stall. Wing loading (weight divided by wing area) sets how fast a bird must fly: a high loading goes with short pointed wings and rapid beats, a low loading with long wings and slow flight. The bird in this model stands still: it is not drawn in flight, and the 3-D wings are folded.

facts: makes lift and provides most of the thrust (Wikipedia, Bird flight)
wing folded slightly inward to reduce the energy cost
feathers of the "thumb" that help avoid stalling at low speed

title: Song, and how a bird sings two notes at once
summary: A robin sings with its syrinx, a voice box at the base of the windpipe that has two sides which can work separately.

layers.basics: A bird does not sing with its throat the way you do. The sound is made deep in the chest, where the windpipe splits in two to go to the lungs. That organ is the syrinx. Because each of the two branches has its own vibrating membranes and its own muscles, the two sides can be controlled separately, and some songbirds use this to make more than one sound at the same time. The mouth and windpipe above then shape the sound.
layers.deeper: In songbirds the syrinx lies where the windpipe forks (the tracheobronchial form). Sound comes from vibration of thin membranes and of the pessulus, a median bony wedge, as air from the lungs passes. Muscles on each bronchus tension the membranes of that side independently; a study of the intact syrinx measured the contributions of the left and right sides separately (Suthers 1990). Songbirds (oscines) have the finest control of these muscles of any birds. Both sexes sing, all year round; the winter song is more plaintive, and a male starts morning song about an hour before sunrise.
layers.expert: The demonstration of independent left and right contributions comes from other songbirds, so it is a statement about songbirds in general. The model's syrinx (cut-open view) is a simplified drawing at true size.

facts: at the fork of the windpipe, above the lungs
starts about an hour before civil sunrise (WR)
open_questions: How much do robins use both sides of the syrinx at once? The independent-sides result comes from other songbirds.

title: Why robins sing at night in cities
summary: In a Sheffield survey, robins sang at night at the places that were noisiest by day; street lights explained little once noise was counted.

layers.basics: A robin that sings at night near a street light is a familiar puzzle. One careful study in the English city of Sheffield found that the places where robins sang at night were the places that were much noisier during the day. Light at night did not explain the pattern once the daytime noise was taken into account.
layers.deeper: The study (Fuller, Warren and Gaston 2007) visited 121 locations once by day and once at night. Robins sang by day at 67 of them and at night at 18 of those. Night-singing sites were louder by day: about 63 dB against about 53 dB. Light was higher at night-singing sites too, but that effect vanished when daytime noise was entered into the analysis. The authors suggest that robins may sing at night to avoid being drowned out by day, or because the night is quiet enough to be heard; their data cannot tell these apart.
layers.expert: A logistic regression gave a significant effect of daytime noise (p = 0.002) and none of light (p = 0.947). Song output per session did not differ between day and night. Other studies have examined light as a cause; how much each of light and noise matters, and whether it differs between cities, is not settled.

facts: ≈ 63 dB at night-singing sites, ≈ 53 dB at day-only sites
open_questions: Is night singing in towns a response to daytime noise, to artificial light, or both? Do the birds sing at night to avoid daytime noise or to use the quiet?

ext.title: Fuller, Warren and Gaston 2007: Daytime noise predicts nocturnal singing in urban robins (Biology Letters)

title: Territory, and the red breast as a signal
summary: A robin defends a territory, and the orange breast is what a rival responds to: in David Lack's experiments a bundle of red feathers could provoke an attack.

layers.basics: Male robins defend a patch of ground fiercely against other males, and sometimes against other small birds and even their own reflection. The orange breast is the signal. David Lack put stuffed robins into the territories of living ones. The residents attacked them, and some birds even attacked a bundle of red feathers on its own.
layers.deeper: Lack's fieldwork was at Dartington Hall; his book The Life of the Robin appeared in 1943. In the account of his experiments, one hen robin attacked the empty space where red feathers had been. Fights are costly: territorial disputes cause up to about 10 % of adult deaths in some areas. Both sexes sing and defend ground, and song is a second signal that tells neighbours where a territory's owner is.
layers.expert: The experiment shows that red feathers released the aggressive response in those birds, which fits the idea that the breast works as a signal of an intruder. It does not by itself show why red evolved or what the breast colour says about the bird, and the details of Lack's original tests are better read in his book than in summaries.

facts: territorial disputes account for up to ≈ 10 % of adult deaths in some areas (WR)
stuffed robins in territories; a bundle of red feathers could provoke attack
open_questions: What does the colour and size of the red patch tell a rival, and how did it evolve as a signal?

ext.title: The robins of Dartington (Great British Life), on David Lack's fieldwork

title: Migration: some robins travel, many stay
summary: British and Irish robins mostly stay put; robins from Scandinavia and Russia move west and south for the winter.

layers.basics: In Britain and Ireland most robins are residents all year. A small minority, mostly females, leave for southern Europe, some as far as Spain. Robins breeding in Scandinavia and Russia are the long-distance ones: they migrate to Britain and western Europe to escape harsher winters, which is why there are more robins in British gardens in winter.
layers.deeper: A population can contain both residents and migrants, so migration is a habit that varies within a species, not a single trait. The robin is also the best-known test animal for the question of how migrating birds keep direction, which leads to the compass card.
layers.expert: The shares of residents and migrants vary between populations and years. Migrants are described as greyer above and duller orange below than residents.

facts: largely resident; a small minority (usually females) goes to southern Europe, some to Spain
migrate to Britain and western Europe for winter

title: Body temperature and heart rate
summary: Birds run hotter than mammals: about 41 °C when active, and a small songbird's heart beats several hundred times a minute.

layers.basics: A robin is warm-blooded and runs hotter than you: birds in general average about 38.5 °C at rest and about 41 °C when active. Its heart is small and very fast. For scale, a similar-sized songbird, the tropical spotted antbird of about 17 g, was measured in the wild at between 260 beats a minute at night and 824 a minute by day.
layers.deeper: In a review of body temperatures in birds, the mean was 38.54 ± 0.96 °C in the resting phase (203 birds), 41.02 ± 1.29 °C in the active phase (724) and 43.85 ± 0.94 °C in high activity (74). Passerines run slightly high in the active phase. The animation of the heart in this model is an illustration with no real rate. For scale, a ruby-throated hummingbird's heart can beat up to 1,200 times a minute.
layers.expert: Heart rate and oxygen use rise together, so a heart-rate record can stand in for the energy a bird spends. Many birds lower their body temperature a little at night as a way to save energy. The antbird numbers are for another species in a rain forest, not a measurement on robins.

open_questions: What is a robin's own heart rate at rest, in flight and in winter? The values on this card are for birds in general and for a similar-sized tropical songbird.

title: How long a robin lives
summary: Most robins die in their first year: the average life expectancy is about 1.1 years, though a few live many years.

layers.basics: Robins have a short average life because so many die in their first year. Birds that reach breeding age typically live about two years. The oldest ringed wild robin on the British record reached 8 years, 4 months and 30 days (ringed bird, 1977). A longer record of 19 years is quoted in other places.
layers.deeper: Life expectancy at the start (about 1.1 years) is much lower than the typical age of birds that survive to breed (about 2 years) because of heavy first-year mortality. Very low winter temperatures raise mortality, and fighting over territory accounts for up to about 10 % of adult deaths in some areas.
layers.expert: The two sources disagree on the record age (8 years 4 months from the British ringing scheme, 19 years in Wikipedia); the card gives both rather than choosing.

facts: Typical age if it reaches breeding
8 years 4 months 30 days (BTO); 19 years quoted by WR
usually 2 a year, 4 to 5 eggs (2 to 9), incubation 14 to 16 days, fledging at 12.5 to 16 days (BTO)
open_questions: Which record is right? The ringing record and the longer quoted age differ.

title: Birds are living dinosaurs
summary: Birds are theropod dinosaurs: the robin is a descendant of feathered dinosaurs that lived over 150 million years ago.

layers.basics: A robin is a dinosaur, in the same way you are a mammal. Birds belong to the theropods, the group that includes Velociraptor and Tyrannosaurus, and many theropods had feathers. Fossils of more than thirty feathered non-bird dinosaurs have been collected, many in Liaoning in China. Features that robins share with those dinosaurs include hollow, air-filled bones, a gizzard, and a habit of nest-building and brooding.
layers.deeper: The present consensus is that birds are maniraptoran theropods that originated in the Mesozoic. Sinosauropteryx (found in 1996) was covered in simple filaments, and later work showed that its filaments had a central shaft with barbs. Anchiornis, a small feathered dinosaur with long arm and leg feathers, lived before Archaeopteryx. Archaeopteryx, from the Late Jurassic limestone of Solnhofen in Germany, is about 155 million years old.
layers.expert: Debated within that consensus: the exact sequence of changes among the maniraptorans; which digits the bird hand keeps (II-III-IV on the embryo, I-II-III in the fossils); whether the earliest flapping evolved from the ground up, from the trees down or with wing-assisted running up slopes. A small minority argues that birds did not come from dinosaurs at all.

facts: more than 30 species with preserved feathers
pneumatic bones, gizzard stones, nest-building, brooding
open_questions: Which digits of the bird hand are which (II-III-IV from embryos, I-II-III from fossils)?
How did flight begin: from the ground up, from the trees down, or by running up slopes?

title: A magnetic compass sense
summary: Robins appear to sense Earth's magnetic field; one idea is that a light-sensitive protein in the eye, cryptochrome, is the sensor. This is not proved.

layers.basics: The European robin is one of the migratory songbirds used to test the idea that birds have a compass in their eyes. The leading hypothesis says that when light hits a protein called cryptochrome, two electrons are moved and a pair of molecules, each with an unpaired electron, forms. Earth's magnetic field, weak as it is, could change how long that pair lasts, and so change a signal the bird sees. Whether this is really how robins sense direction is an open question.
layers.deeper: In 2021 Xu and colleagues reported that cryptochrome 4 from the European robin, made in the laboratory, has a chain of four tryptophan amino-acid residues along which light moves electrons in four steps, forming four radical pairs. Radicals lasting more than 100 nanoseconds were found, long enough to be sensitive to a magnetic field, and the protein carries its flavin (FAD) fully. The results are from purified protein in a test tube; conditions in a living eye differ, and the work did not show the effect in a bird.
layers.expert: The radical-pair mechanism is accepted as real chemistry. What is unproved is that cryptochrome 4 in the robin's eye is the compass, how the radical pairs would be read out by the nervous system, and how the weak signal survives the noisy environment of a living cell. Tests would need to link the molecule to the bird's behaviour.

facts: four, along a tryptophan chain (in vitro)
over 100 ns in the wild-type protein (in vitro)
hypothesis: not shown in a living bird
open_questions: Is cryptochrome 4 the robin's magnetic sensor in the living eye?
How is a magnetically sensitive chemical signal read out by the nerves, and how does it survive in a living cell?

title: Keratin: the protein of feathers, bill and claws
summary: Feathers, beak and claws are made of beta-keratin, a tough protein held together by sulfur bridges between cysteine units.

layers.basics: The hard, light stuff of a feather is a protein called keratin. In birds and reptiles it is a special kind, beta-keratin, built of sheets that are twisted together and locked by sulfur-to-sulfur bridges. Those bridges come from the amino acid cysteine. The keratin molecule itself is not in this explorer's molecule data; its building block, cysteine, and the linked pair, cystine, are.
layers.deeper: Beta-keratins are found only in birds and reptiles. In feathers, beaks and claws they are formed mainly as beta-pleated sheets, stabilised by disulfide bridges between cysteine residues. Hair and horn in mammals are made of a different protein family, alpha-keratin. Because a bridge cannot be undone without a chemical reaction, a feather is a long-lived, heat-stable material.
layers.expert: The sauropsid beta-keratins are encoded by a different gene family from alpha-keratins; the name "corneous beta proteins" has been proposed to avoid the confusion. Human hair is about 14 % cysteine for comparison (not measured on feathers).

title: What colours the robin's feathers
summary: Brown feathers get their colour from melanin; the orange of the breast is classed as melanin-based in one study, but its pigment has not been shown by chemical analysis.

layers.basics: Feather colour comes from pigments and from structure. The two common pigment groups are melanins (browns and blacks) and carotenoids (reds, oranges and yellows that a bird gets from its food). The robin's brown back is melanin. For the orange breast, a study that measured the colour of four European songbirds grouped the robin's breast with the melanin-based colours; the authors say this is the main mechanism and that the classification rested on the usual understanding, not on chemical tests.
layers.deeper: The paper (Delhey and colleagues 2010) measured 236 robin samples over three years. It suggests that a red feather may be coloured by phaeomelanin, the reddish form of melanin, which is the dominant pigment in many red plumages. A carotenoid colour cannot be ruled out without extracting the pigment from robin breast feathers. For that reason this explorer does not draw a carotenoid molecule here.
layers.expert: Melanin is made from the amino acid tyrosine through L-DOPA; the molecule data has L-DOPA, tyrosine, and also beta-carotene, which is only an example of the carotenoid group. Birds cannot make carotenoids and take them in food; whether a robin does so for its breast is not shown.

facts: classed melanin-based; pigment not tested by chemistry
open_questions: Which pigment colours the robin's orange breast: phaeomelanin, a carotenoid, or both? It needs chemical analysis of the feathers.

ext.title: Delhey et al. 2010: Seasonal changes in colour (PLoS ONE; robin, blackbird, blue tit, great tit)

title: How a robin breathes: air that flows one way
summary: A bird's lungs are fed by air sacs, so air flows through the lung in one direction, in and out, and a single breath stays in the body for two breath cycles.

layers.basics: You breathe in and out through the same tubes, and the air in your lungs goes back and forth. A bird does not. Air passes through its lungs in one direction all the time, because the lungs are connected to a set of balloon-like air sacs that act as bellows. Fresh air goes first to the sacs at the back, then through the lung, then to the sacs at the front, and out. A little of each breath is in the bird for two breath cycles before it is breathed out.
layers.deeper: The air sacs do not exchange gas themselves; the lung tubes (parabronchi) do. Aerodynamic valves and narrowing of the airways keep the flow in one direction, so the lung gets fresh air during both the breathing-in and the breathing-out. In a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and yellow-headed blackbirds, the anterior sacs were ventilated differently during calling and flapping, and the tracer reached the front sacs faster than the simple model predicts, so the picture still has details to be worked out.
layers.expert: Birds have typically nine air sacs (range 7 to 12). Wikipedia says passerines have seven, so descriptions differ. The model draws nine in the usual textbook arrangement.

facts: typically nine (range 7 to 12); the model draws nine
stays about two breath cycles (duck model)
Breathing rate in the tracer-gas study
calling raised it from 1.5 to 2.3 breaths per second; wing flapping reached 3.5
open_questions: How exactly do valves and airway shapes keep the flow in one direction, and how do the front sacs behave during calling and flapping?

title: How a robin keeps hold of a twig
summary: A tendon behind the ankle tightens when the leg bends, curling the toes round a perch with little effort.

layers.basics: A bird can stand on a twig all night without tiring. When it squats, the ankle bends and a long tendon is pulled tight; the tendon pulls the toes shut around the perch. The tendon and the tissue around it are rough, which locks the grip until the leg straightens again. The ankle is the joint that looks like a backward knee. In the standing pose shown here, the toes rest flat on the boulder, so the lock is not engaged.
layers.deeper: A robin's foot has three toes pointing forward (toes II, III and IV) and one back (the hind toe, toe I): the usual arrangement in perching birds and nearly all songbirds. The toe bones number 3, 4 and 5 in the three forward toes and 2 in the hind toe.
layers.expert: A 2012 study of European starlings found that sleeping birds bent their knees only slightly, not enough to engage the lock, and balanced on the central pad of the foot, so the lock may matter less than the popular explanation says.

facts: the joint between the tibiotarsus and tarsometatarsus
open_questions: How much do birds depend on the tendon lock while perching and sleeping?

title: Hollow bones with struts
summary: Many bird bones are hollow and air-filled, braced inside by thin struts: light, but stiff.

layers.basics: A bird's skeleton has to be light enough to fly. Many of its bones are hollow tubes filled with air, with thin struts across the inside like the braces in a bridge. The air comes from the air sacs, which reach into some bones. A feathered bird's plumage can weigh two or three times as much as its skeleton. Not every bird has hollow bones: penguins, loons, puffins and kiwis do not.
layers.deeper: Pneumatised bones are shared with the theropod dinosaurs that birds came from. In a tube, strength comes from the wall and from the distance of material from the axis, so a thin hollow wall can match a solid rod of much greater mass.
layers.expert: The extent of pneumatisation differs between species and between bones; in small songbirds some bones carry little air. How far pneumatisation reaches in a small songbird varies from bone to bone; the tissue scene is a general picture of a hollow bird bone, not a measurement on a robin.

facts: plumage can weigh 2 to 3 times as much as the skeleton (WFE)

title: Crown
summary: The top of the head: olive-brown, running back from just above the forehead.

layers.basics: The crown is brown, with an olive tinge in British birds, and sits like a cap above the orange face. Click a part and look at the layer buttons to see what lies under it: skin, then the skull.
layers.deeper: The head feathers are small contour feathers laid like tiles. Like those of the nape and back, they are coloured by melanin. Young robins are spotted brown and white, and the orange appears gradually.
layers.expert: The borders between the brown crown and the orange face and the grey neck are drawn jagged on purpose; in life they are the edges of feather tracts and the feathers overlap.

facts: spotted brown and white; orange appears gradually (WR)

title: Nape and neck
summary: The back of the head and the neck: olive-brown, over the long neck bones.

layers.basics: The nape is the back of the neck. It is brown like the crown and back. Under the feathers lies a long, flexible neck: a songbird has 14 neck vertebrae, twice as many as a person.
layers.deeper: The feathers sit in rows (tracts) on bare skin between them. The neck lets the robin turn its head far back to preen and to look along its body with each eye.
layers.expert: The neck is covered by contour feathers and downy feathers beneath; the model draws only one smooth outline for the neck feathers.

facts: 14 in all but 2 of 159 songbirds in a study of 47 species (Webster and Goff)

title: Face and throat
summary: The orange face, chin and throat: the front of the signal patch, edged with grey on the sides of the neck.

layers.basics: The face is orange from the forehead and the eye down to the chin and throat, and runs on into the breast. Males and females look alike. The eye sits in the orange, with a thin pale ring round it.
layers.deeper: In Lack's experiments a bundle of red feathers could provoke territorial attack, so the orange front of a robin is treated as a signal to rivals. How the pigment is made is not proved (see the colour card).
layers.expert: The face is made of small feathers that end in bristle-like tips around the bill base (rictal bristles) in many birds; the model draws only the smooth outline.

facts: orange face and breast, edged with bluish grey (WR)

title: Breast
summary: The orange breast: the robin's famous signal, bordered by grey at the sides.

layers.basics: This is the orange-red that gives the robin its name. It sits over the large flight muscles of the breast. Rivals read it as a threat, and a bundle of red feathers alone could provoke an attack in Lack's experiments.
layers.deeper: The breast feathers overlap like roof tiles and are thick enough to hold a layer of air against the skin. Their colour was classed as melanin-based by Delhey et al. 2010, without a chemical test.
layers.expert: Under the feathers and skin the large pectoral muscles cover the keeled breastbone. The shape of the breast changes as the bird fluffs its feathers.

facts: a bundle of red feathers could provoke attack (Lack)

title: Grey border of the breast
summary: A band of bluish grey between the orange breast and the brown back, on the sides of the neck and chest.

layers.basics: The orange face and breast are edged on the sides of the neck and chest with bluish grey. The grey makes the orange stand out.
layers.deeper: Grey in feathers is usually a dilute black melanin. Blue-looking colours in feathers can also come from fine structure that scatters light, so the origin of the blue tinge is a separate question.
layers.expert: The colour in the model is a flat grey; the real band is feathered and graded.

title: Back (mantle and scapulars)
summary: The olive-brown upper back and the long shoulder feathers that cover the folded wing's root.

layers.basics: The back is olive-brown: camouflage when the robin is on the ground or in a hedge. Its folded wings lie over the sides of it.
layers.deeper: The scapular feathers are long feathers growing along the shoulder blade; they lie over the base of the folded wing.
layers.expert: The brown is melanin-based in the Delhey et al. 2010 classification.

title: Rump
summary: The lower back above the tail, where the tail feathers are anchored.

layers.basics: The rump is the rear of the back, just in front of the tail. Under its feathers the fused hip bones and the stub of the tail bones lie.
layers.deeper: The upper tail coverts spring from here and cover the roots of the tail feathers. The preen gland (uropygial gland) of many birds lies on the rump; it is not drawn in this model.
layers.expert: The rump plumage is slightly warmer brown in the model.

facts: plumage over the pelvis, the base of the tail

title: Flank
summary: The side of the body between the wing and the belly: buff-brown.

layers.basics: The flank is the side of the belly, below the folded wing and above the leg. The thigh is hidden under these feathers; only the lower leg shows.
layers.deeper: The leg has a "knee" hidden in the flank plumage: what looks like a backward knee below it is the ankle.
layers.expert: Flank feathers are loose and fluff out; they help insulate the thigh.

title: Belly
summary: The pale belly: whitish, in contrast with the orange breast above it.

layers.basics: The belly is whitish. It covers the soft organs: the gizzard, liver and intestines, with the air sacs round them.
layers.deeper: The belly feathers are denser at the sides; a bird in cold weather fluffs them to trap air.
layers.expert: Under the belly lies the posterior part of the body cavity; the keel of the breastbone does not reach the rear.

title: Vent and undertail area
summary: The feathers round the single opening for gut, kidneys and reproduction, the cloaca.

layers.basics: The vent is the area around the cloaca: birds use one opening for droppings, urine and reproduction. The feathers of the undertail cover the base of the tail from below.
layers.deeper: The kidneys excrete nitrogen as uric acid, which is semi-solid; it leaves with the faeces.
layers.expert: The cloaca is also the opening of the reproductive tract; the same opening serves the reproductive tract.

title: Bill: upper and lower mandible
summary: The bill is a thin, pointed horny sheath over the jaw bones: the robin's tweezers for picking up small food.

layers.basics: The bill has two halves, the upper and lower mandible. They are covered with a hard, horny sheath of keratin and are black in a robin. A robin uses its bill like tweezers to pick up small food. Birds have no teeth: the bill and the gizzard do the work.
layers.deeper: The horn sheath is a living tissue that grows continuously and wears at the tip. Inside, the upper jaw is a slender bone (the premaxilla) fused to the skull, and the lower jaw hinges at the quadrate bone. The nostrils open on the top of the upper mandible near its base.
layers.expert: The sheath is beta-keratin, like feathers and claws. Birds can move the upper jaw a little on the skull (cranial kinesis), a trait that varies by group; its extent in robins is not described here.

title: Nostrils
summary: The two small openings in the upper bill near its base, through which air reaches the nose.

layers.basics: Birds breathe in through two small nostrils, near the base of the upper bill. They lead into the nasal cavity and then down the windpipe.
layers.deeper: The openings are often partly covered by feathers or a flap. They are not at the tip of the bill, as in a mammal, but at its base, so that the bill can probe without clogging them.
layers.expert: The nostrils are drawn as small ovals at true size.

title: Eye
summary: A robin's eye is dark and large for the size of its head.

layers.basics: The black bead you see is the front of the eye: the dark pupil and the iris round it. The whole eyeball is about 8 mm across in the model and fills much of the head. Each eye points sideways, so the robin sees a wide area at once, and it turns its head to look at things with both eyes.
layers.deeper: The cut-open view shows the layers: the cornea, the iris, the lens, the vitreous, the retina, and the pecten, a pleated fold that is only found in birds. Click the retina to look inside it.
layers.expert: The eye is drawn about 8 mm across; the real size varies by individual. The visible dark dome in the plumage is the cornea and pupil; the iris is dark brown to black in a robin.

title: Eye ring
summary: A thin pale ring round the eye: the rim of the eyelids with a ring of tiny feathers.

layers.basics: Many birds have a ring round the eye, made of the eyelid rim and small feathers. In a robin it is faint. A bird has three eyelids: an upper, a lower, and a see-through one (the nictitating membrane) that sweeps across the eye from the corner.
layers.deeper: The lower lid moves more than the upper in most birds. The third eyelid cleans and protects the eye and can be drawn across it in flight.
layers.expert: The ring is drawn as a thin tube; in life it is graded and feathered.

facts: upper, lower and a see-through third

title: Wing: the arm that became a wing
summary: A bird's wing is an arm: the same bones as ours, with the wrist and hand fused and the fingers reduced, and feathers in place of skin.

layers.basics: Fold your arm and compare. The wing has an upper arm bone (humerus), two forearm bones (radius and ulna), and a hand. The wrist and hand bones are fused into one hand bone, and only three fingers remain, one of them carrying the alula. The big feathers are attached to the forearm and hand bones. Use the "Cut open: the wing" view to see the bones and compare them with the human arm.
layers.deeper: Bones and muscles are the same family as ours; evolution kept the pattern and changed the proportions. The primaries are attached to the hand, the secondaries to the forearm, the tertials near the elbow; coverts overlay their roots. Muscles in the chest move the whole wing; very few muscles lie in the wing itself, which keeps the wing light.
layers.expert: Which three digits the bird hand keeps is debated: the fossils suggest I-II-III, the embryo II-III-IV. The model draws the bones of the folded wing in simplified form.

facts: 10 in most passerines, the outermost tiny (WFF, Pyle)
humerus, radius, ulna, fused hand bone, three fingers

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Primaries: the main flight feathers
summary: The primaries are the long flight feathers of the hand, the main thrust of a wing; most songbirds have ten, the outermost small.

layers.basics: These are the long, stiff feathers at the tip of the wing. They are attached to the hand and do most of the work of flying. A robin has ten, of which the outermost is tiny; the model draws all ten per wing, overlapping like the slats of a blind. Click one to read how it is built.
layers.deeper: Each feather has a central shaft, the rachis, with a flat vane on each side made of side branches (barbs), which carry smaller branches (barbules) with tiny hooks. The hooks fasten neighbouring barbs together like Velcro, so the vane is a smooth surface that air cannot pass through. The base of the shaft, the hollow quill (calamus), sits in the skin and is anchored by ligaments to the bone.
layers.expert: Most modern passerines have ten primaries, and a few have only nine, lacking the tiny outer one. Each primary can be replaced in moult. The vane, rachis and barbules are made of beta-keratin.

facts: 10 in most modern passerines; the outermost is tiny
8 to 16 µm between neighbouring barbules on flight feathers of species from a hummingbird to a condor (J. R. Soc. Interface 2025)

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts
The feather's multi-functional structure across nano to macro scales inspires hierarchical design (J. R. Soc. Interface 22(225), 2025)

title: Secondaries
summary: The secondaries are the flight feathers of the forearm; a passerine has nine including three tertials.

layers.basics: The secondaries make up the inner part of the wing and form its broad surface. They are attached to the forearm bone, the ulna. A robin has nine in all, counting the three innermost ones, the tertials. The model draws six secondaries.
layers.deeper: Together the secondaries and primaries make a continuous, curved surface. The secondaries are symmetrical and shorter than the primaries, built for lift more than thrust.
layers.expert: In passerines the secondaries number nine counting the tertials; other birds range from six (hummingbirds) to as many as 40 (some albatrosses).

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Tertials
summary: The three innermost secondaries, which lie over the folded wing like a roof.

layers.basics: The tertials are the three feathers nearest the body, attached near the elbow. When the wing is folded they cover the bases of the primaries and the elbow.
layers.deeper: Technically the tertials are part of the secondary tract; they differ in having shafts set into the tissue near the elbow joint rather than into the ulna.
layers.expert: They are drawn shorter and broader than the other secondaries.

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Coverts: small feathers over the flight feathers
summary: The coverts are short feathers that cover the shafts of the flight feathers and smooth the wing surface; there are several rows.

layers.basics: Over the roots of the long feathers lie rows of shorter ones: the primary coverts, the greater, median and lesser coverts. They protect the shafts and smooth the airflow. In first-winter robins the tips of the coverts are yellow-brown and more obvious, which helps tell young birds from old.
layers.deeper: Coverts lie above and below the flight feathers: at least one layer on each side. In the model each of the four groups is drawn, from the long greater coverts to the small lesser coverts, as a set of overlapping blades.
layers.expert: The counts of coverts in each row are drawn to make the rows look right; they are not measured counts.

title: Alula
summary: The alula is a small group of feathers on the bird's "thumb", used like a slat on an aircraft wing for slow flight and landing.

layers.basics: The alula is a few small feathers at the front of the wrist. When a bird slows down to land, it lifts the alula and the air stays smoothly attached to the wing instead of breaking away. The model draws three.
layers.deeper: The alula is borne by the first finger. It is not a flight feather in the strict sense, but it acts like the slats on an airplane wing, which keep lift at high angles of attack.
layers.expert: The alula works like a leading-edge slat; the number of its feathers varies by species, and three are drawn.

facts: avoids stalling at low speed, as when landing (WFF; Bird flight)

title: Rachis: the shaft of a feather
summary: The rachis is the stiff, tapering central shaft of a feather, with the vane growing out on each side.

layers.basics: The rachis runs the length of the feather. It is a light, springy rod that bends and springs back. Below the vane it becomes the hollow quill that fits into the skin.
layers.deeper: The barbs are fused to the rachis in a row on each side. The rachis is thickest at the base, where it is cylindrical and hollow, and tapers to the tip.
layers.expert: It is made of beta-keratin. In the model it is drawn as a thin tube, scaled by the feather length.

title: Tail feathers (12)
summary: The tail is a fan of twelve long feathers, which steers and brakes the bird in flight.

layers.basics: Most passerines have twelve tail feathers, six on each side, and so does a robin. They are called rectrices (the singular is rectrix). The middle pair lies on top when the tail is closed. In flight the tail spreads to give lift and to steer. The feathers are anchored to the pygostyle, a small plate of fused tail bones.
layers.deeper: The tail feathers are held by a pad of muscle and fat at the base. Their count is not fixed in all birds: some passerines have 10, 8 or even 6, the superb lyrebird has 16.
layers.expert: In the model the tail is drawn closed, with twelve feathers lying in a slightly rounded fan.

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Tail coverts
summary: Short feathers that cover the roots of the tail feathers from above and below.

layers.basics: Over and under the base of the tail, rows of shorter feathers cover the roots of the twelve tail feathers. The upper ones are brown like the back; the under ones are pale buff.
layers.deeper: Like the wing coverts, they smooth the airflow and protect the shafts, with at least one layer above and below.
layers.expert: Two rows each are drawn; the number is approximate.

facts: upper and under, two drawn each

title: Shin (tibiotarsus)
summary: The lowest part of the shin, where the long leg bone comes out of the belly feathers.

layers.basics: The upper leg of a bird is hidden by the body feathers: the thigh bone and the knee are inside. What shows first is the shin, the tibiotarsus, which is the shin bone fused with some ankle bones. It is covered with a feathered or smooth skin that runs down to the ankle.
layers.deeper: The tibiotarsus is the longest leg bone of a robin. Its muscles, in the shin, sit high, close to the body, and long tendons run down to the toes, so the lower leg is light and thin.
layers.expert: The shape and length of the visible shin depend on how the belly feathers are fluffed.

facts: tibiotarsus: tibia fused with proximal tarsal bones

title: Ankle: the "backward knee"
summary: The joint that looks like a backward knee is the ankle; the real knee is hidden in the belly feathers.

layers.basics: The bend in a bird's leg that points backward is not the knee. It is the ankle (the heel). Birds walk on their toes, so their foot bones, the tarsus, are long and stand almost upright. The true knee is hidden in the feathers higher up and bends forward like yours.
layers.deeper: The ankle is the joint between the tibiotarsus and the tarsometatarsus. When a perching bird squats, bending the ankle tightens the toe-flexor tendon that runs behind it and curls the toes around the perch.
layers.expert: The ankle (intertarsal) joint is a hinge. It is drawn as a small ball.

title: Tarsus: the scaly foot bone
summary: The tarsus is the long, scaly part of the leg, a foot bone that has become a leg segment.

layers.basics: What looks like the lower leg of a bird is part of its foot. The long, thin tarsus is the fused foot bones (the tarsometatarsus), covered in horny scales. It adds an extra segment to the leg and lengthens the stride.
layers.deeper: The tarsometatarsus is a segment specific to birds; it gives the leg extra lever length. A robin has long legs for a bird of its size and hops on the ground.
layers.expert: The tarsus is a straight rod with faint rings for the scales; real scales are in rows called scutes.

facts: tarsometatarsus: fused foot bones, specific to birds (Wikipedia)

title: Toes: three forward, one back
summary: A robin's foot has three toes pointing forward and one pointing back, the usual arrangement of a perching bird.

layers.basics: Three toes point forward and one, the hind toe or hallux, points back. This is the arrangement of nearly all songbirds and most other perching birds, called anisodactyl. The toes have 3, 4 and 5 bones in the inner, middle and outer front toes and 2 in the hind toe.
layers.deeper: On a branch, the toes close around the perch from front and back. In this model the bird stands on a boulder, so its toes are spread on the rock.
layers.expert: The toe bones number 3, 4, 5 and 2 in a typical perching bird. The model draws them with bones of that number.

facts: anisodactyl: toes II, III, IV forward, toe I back

title: Hind toe (hallux)
summary: The single toe pointing backward: the one that closes against the front toes in a perching grip.

layers.basics: The hind toe points backward and is the first toe, the equivalent of our big toe. It is strong and ends in a long claw. When the robin perches, it closes against the three front toes.
layers.deeper: It has two bones. The claw is longer than those of the front toes.
layers.expert: Drawn with a long, curved claw.

title: Claws
summary: Each toe ends in a curved claw, a sheath of keratin over the last toe bone.

layers.basics: The claws are the horny nails of the toes, strong enough to grip bark and rock. They are made of keratin like feathers and the bill, and they grow and wear.
layers.deeper: Each claw is a sheath of keratin over the last bone of the toe, as a human nail covers the end of a finger.
layers.expert: The curve is drawn by eye.

title: Skin
summary: The robin's skin is thin and light, and bare between the feather tracts.

layers.basics: Under the feathers a bird's skin is thin. Feathers grow from small pits (follicles) in rows. Between the rows the skin is bare, which lets the feathers be raised and lowered by tiny muscles.
layers.deeper: Feathers, bill and claws are skin structures made of keratin, in the way that hair and nails are for us.
layers.expert: The model draws the skin as a thin shell. The real skin varies in thickness from place to place.

facts: feathers, bill sheath, claws, scales of the legs

title: Muscles
summary: The robin's muscles: the very large flight muscles of the breast, with smaller muscles in the neck, back, wing, tail and legs.

layers.basics: A flying bird puts most of its muscle in the breast, close to the centre of the body, so that the wings are light. Muscle drives everything the robin does: beating the wing, turning the head, hopping, and singing.
layers.deeper: Click a muscle to read what it does. The flight muscles are the pectoralis and supracoracoideus.
layers.expert: The muscle shapes are schematic, drawn as simple solids.

title: Soft tissue (a stand-in)
summary: In the cut view the pale pink between the organs is a stand-in for fat, connective tissue and the many small parts that are not drawn.

layers.basics: A real bird has no empty spaces inside: between the organs there are fat, connective tissue and fluid. In the cut-open view the model fills the gaps with a pale pink shape so that the cut looks solid. It is a drawing aid and not a tissue.
layers.deeper: The fill is a closed shape set a few millimetres inside the skin.
layers.expert: It carries no information about the real tissue.

title: Skeleton
summary: A bird's skeleton is light and fused: hollow bones, a keeled breastbone, a wishbone, a fused hand, a long neck.

layers.basics: The skeleton holds the robin up and gives the muscles something to pull on. In a bird, many bones that are separate in us are fused into one: the hand, the hip and lower back, the tail tip. The breastbone carries a deep keel and the two collarbones are fused into a wishbone.
layers.deeper: Click a bone to read what it is and what it is in a human. A robin has a long neck of 14 bones, very few teeth (none), and ribs with little hooks.
layers.expert: The bone shapes are drawn as simplified rods and plates.

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Organs
summary: The robin's organs: heart, liver, stomach and gizzard, intestines, kidneys, eyes, with the lungs and air sacs shown separately.

layers.basics: Inside the body lie the heart, the liver, a two-part stomach, the intestines and the kidneys. A bird has no teeth and no bladder; it grinds food in a muscular stomach, the gizzard, and passes uric acid with its droppings through one opening, the cloaca.
layers.deeper: Click an organ to see what it is. The lungs and the air sacs are in their own layer.
layers.expert: Organ shapes, sizes and positions are approximate.

title: Pectoralis: the downstroke muscle
summary: The pectoralis is the robin's biggest muscle, a sheet over the breast that pulls the wing down.

layers.basics: The pectoralis lies on each side of the keel, over the ribs and the underside of the breast. When it contracts it pulls the wing down, and the downstroke makes most of the lift and thrust of a beat. This is why a bird has such a plump breast.
layers.deeper: The muscle runs from the keel and the wishbone to the humerus, on its crest. It is the muscle bird-lovers mean by "breast". It is made of fibres packed with mitochondria that supply the energy of flight; click the muscle's scene to look inside.
layers.expert: The pectoralis is the larger of the two flight muscles. It is drawn as a thick sheet over the sternum; its size is schematic.

title: Supracoracoideus: the upstroke muscle
summary: The supracoracoideus lies under the pectoralis, yet it lifts the wing, by pulling a tendon over the shoulder like a rope over a pulley.

layers.basics: It would be natural to put the muscle that lifts the wing on the bird's back, but the supracoracoideus lies on the breast, beside the keel, under the pectoralis. A long tendon runs from it up through a gap in the shoulder, the triosseal canal, and over the top to the humerus. The gap acts as a pulley: a pull down in the breast becomes a lift of the wing.
layers.deeper: The muscle is the smaller of the two flight muscles. Keeping both heavy muscles low in the body, near the centre of gravity, keeps the bird stable. This arrangement is a feature of modern birds; early birds such as Archaeopteryx may have lacked it.
layers.expert: The tendon passes through the triosseal canal, formed by the coracoid, the scapula and the wishbone. The canal is drawn as a small ring in the cut-open wing view.

facts: the triosseal canal at the shoulder

title: Tendon of the supracoracoideus
summary: The strong cord that carries the pull of the upstroke muscle over the shoulder to the top of the wing bone.

layers.basics: A tendon is a tough cord that joins muscle to bone. This one starts in the supracoracoideus on the breast, passes up through the shoulder pulley, and ends on the humerus.
layers.deeper: Because the tendon is long, the heavy muscle can stay in the breast and only a light cord runs to the wing.
layers.expert: Drawn as a thin tube along its true route in outline.

facts: muscle, triosseal canal, top of the humerus

title: Triosseal canal: the shoulder pulley
summary: A gap between three bones of the shoulder through which the upstroke tendon runs.

layers.basics: Three bones meet at the shoulder: the coracoid, the scapula and the wishbone. They leave a small opening, the triosseal canal ("three-bone canal"). The tendon of the upstroke muscle runs through it, so that the pull is turned from downward to upward.
layers.deeper: It works as a pulley and lets both big flight muscles sit low on the breast.
layers.expert: The ring in the model marks the canal; it is simplified.

title: Neck, back and tail muscles
summary: Long muscles along the neck and back that hold the head and body steady, and a pair at the base of the tail.

layers.basics: A bird's head weighs little but its neck is long and flexible. Long muscles along the neck and back move the head and keep the trunk rigid in flight. Short muscles at the base of the tail steer the tail feathers.
layers.deeper: The neck has 14 bones; the back is stiff because many of its bones are fused.
layers.expert: Drawn as simple tubes and blobs.

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Jaw muscle
summary: The muscle that closes the lower jaw, a pad behind and below the eye.

layers.basics: The jaw muscle lies on the side of the head, behind the eye, and pulls the lower jaw shut. A robin's bill is a delicate tweezer, so this muscle is small.
layers.deeper: The jaw hinges at the quadrate bone on each side of the skull.
layers.expert: Drawn as an ellipsoid.

title: Wing muscles
summary: Small, slim muscles in the upper and lower arm that fold and unfold the wing; the big ones are in the breast.

layers.basics: The wing itself has few muscles: the big flight muscles are in the chest, and long tendons run to the wing. The small muscles in the arm fold and spread the wing and adjust the angle of the feathers.
layers.deeper: Keeping weight out of the wing makes it easier to flap.
layers.expert: Drawn as two tapering muscle bellies on each side.

title: Thigh muscles
summary: The thick thigh muscles, inside the belly feathers, that swing the leg.

layers.basics: The legs of a bird are thin below but powerful above. The thigh muscles are hidden under the belly feathers; they drive hopping and take off.
layers.deeper: Long tendons run from the muscles to the toes.
layers.expert: Drawn as a capsule from the hip to the knee.

facts: hip to knee, hidden under feathers

title: Shank muscles
summary: Muscles of the shin that move the foot by long tendons.

layers.basics: The muscles that curl the toes and extend the foot lie high on the shin, near the knee, so the lower leg can be thin and light. Long tendons run down the back of the ankle.
layers.deeper: The toe-flexor tendon is the one that locks the toes on a perch.
layers.expert: Drawn as a tapering capsule.

title: Tail muscles
summary: Small muscles at the root of the tail that spread, fold and tilt the tail feathers.

layers.basics: The twelve tail feathers are held by a pad of muscle and fat at the base, round the pygostyle. These muscles can spread the tail like a fan and swing it up and down.
layers.deeper: The pygostyle gives them a rigid anchor.
layers.expert: Two small ellipsoids are drawn.

title: Perching tendon
summary: A long tendon runs behind the ankle to the toes; bending the ankle tightens it and curls the toes without effort.

layers.basics: This is the tendon that makes a perch grip easy. It runs from the shin muscles, behind the ankle joint and down the back of the foot, where it splits to the toes. When the ankle bends, the tendon is stretched and pulls the toes shut. The tendon and the tissue around it are rough, so the grip holds until the leg straightens.
layers.deeper: Because the lock needs no continuous muscle effort, a bird can hold on while resting.
layers.expert: In the model the tendon is drawn with ridges where it passes the ankle, to stand for the rough surface; the real ridges and sheath are finer.

facts: shin muscle, behind the ankle, down the back of the foot, to the toes
open_questions: How much do birds rely on the lock while perching and sleeping? A study of starlings found sleeping birds did not bend the leg enough to engage it.

ext.title: Why don't birds fall off branches when they sleep (Science ABC)

title: Skull
summary: A light, toothless skull with huge eye sockets.

layers.basics: The skull is a thin shell of fused bone with no teeth. Most of its side is taken by the two eye sockets (orbits). The bill is the jaw bones sheathed in horn.
layers.deeper: The braincase holds the brain; behind the eyes, the jaw muscles attach. The skull sits on the first neck vertebra by one round joint, which lets the head turn far.
layers.expert: Drawn as a smooth braincase with two sockets; sutures are not shown.

title: Upper jaw bone
summary: The slender bone inside the upper half of the bill.

layers.basics: The upper bill has a bone core, the premaxilla, covered with a sheath of horn. The two nostrils open on it.
layers.deeper: The bone is fused to the skull.
layers.expert: Drawn as a thin cone.

title: Lower jaw bone
summary: The two-pronged bone of the lower bill, hinged on each side of the skull.

layers.basics: The lower jaw is made of two slender bones, joined at the tip, that hinge on the skull at the quadrate bones. A horny sheath covers it.
layers.deeper: In humans the lower jaw hinges directly on the skull; in a bird a separate bone, the quadrate, sits in the hinge.
layers.expert: Drawn as two thin rods.

title: Neck vertebrae (14)
summary: A songbird's neck has 14 vertebrae, twice as many as a person's.

layers.basics: A robin's neck is flexible because it has 14 small vertebrae, where a human has seven. The neck lets the bird reach its whole body with its bill to preen, and turn its head far to look back.
layers.deeper: In a study of 159 songbird skeletons from 47 species, all but two had 14 neck vertebrae, counting the last two, which carry short floating ribs (the cervico-dorsal vertebrae). Birds in general range from 8 to as many as 25 (swans).
layers.expert: The model draws 14 beads. Vertebrae 13 and 14 carry small floating ribs in most songbirds; these are not drawn.

facts: 14 in all but 2 of 159 songbirds (Webster and Goff)

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Chest vertebrae
summary: The vertebrae of the back that carry the ribs.

layers.basics: The vertebrae of the chest carry the ribs. In birds they are stiffer than in us, so the body is a rigid frame that the wings can pull against.
layers.deeper: In a house sparrow the ribs that join the breastbone are on vertebrae 15 to 18; one or two more ribs hang from the front of the fused hip bone.
layers.expert: The model draws five beads.

facts: 4 in a house sparrow (Webster and Goff)

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Synsacrum: the fused lower back and hip
summary: The lower back and hip bones are fused into one rigid piece, the synsacrum.

layers.basics: In a bird many vertebrae of the lower back and hip are fused into a single bone, the synsacrum, together with the hip bones. It makes a stiff, strong platform for the legs, and a stiff trunk helps in flight.
layers.deeper: In birds in general it includes one thoracic, six lumbar, two sacral and five sacro-caudal vertebrae fused to the hip bone (ilium). In songbirds the front part includes three or four thoracodorsal vertebrae.
layers.expert: Drawn as a tapering bar with a flat plate on each side.

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Tail vertebrae
summary: A short chain of free tail bones between the hip and the pygostyle.

layers.basics: A robin has only a few free tail bones, and they end in the pygostyle. A house sparrow has six free tail vertebrae (a figure in a songbird skeleton study); the model draws six.
layers.deeper: These bones give the tail some movement near its root.
layers.expert: Drawn as six small beads.

facts: 6 in a house sparrow (Webster and Goff)

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Pygostyle: the tail plate
summary: The last tail bones are fused into a small plate, the pygostyle, which holds the tail feathers.

layers.basics: Unlike a mammal, a bird has no long tail of bones. The last few tail vertebrae are fused into a flat plate called the pygostyle ("rump pole"), and the tail feathers are fastened round it. The tail is feathers, not bone.
layers.deeper: The pygostyle is formed from the last four caudal vertebrae, although some sources say up to ten.
layers.expert: Drawn as a small plate.

facts: the last ≈ 4 (up to 10 by some counts) (WBA)

title: Breastbone with its keel
summary: The breastbone carries a deep keel, a blade that the flight muscles are anchored to.

layers.basics: The sternum is a broad plate with a deep ridge down the middle, the keel, like the keel of a boat. The big flight muscles are attached on both sides of it. Flightless birds such as ostriches have no keel.
layers.deeper: A deeper keel gives more area for muscle. The keel gives the breast its shape in a plucked bird.
layers.expert: The keel and the plate are drawn smooth; the real sternum has notches and a hole pattern that differ by species.

facts: carries the flight muscles; absent in ostriches (WBA)

title: Wishbone (furcula)
summary: The two collarbones are fused into a V or U, the wishbone, which springs as the wings beat.

layers.basics: A bird's collarbones are joined into one bone, the furcula or wishbone. Birds are the only living vertebrates with fused collarbones. It braces the shoulders apart against the pull of the flight muscles and can flex like a spring.
layers.deeper: Humans have two separate collarbones.
layers.expert: Drawn as a U.

facts: only in birds among living vertebrates (WBA)

title: Coracoids and shoulder blades
summary: The coracoid is a strong strut from the shoulder to the breastbone; the shoulder blade is a slender blade along the ribs.

layers.basics: The coracoids brace the shoulder against the breastbone and take the force of the wing beat. The shoulder blades are long and thin and lie along the back of the ribs. Together with the wishbone they make the shoulder pulley.
layers.deeper: In humans the coracoid is a small hook on the shoulder blade.
layers.expert: Drawn as rods.

title: Ribs and their hooks
summary: The ribs have small hooks, the uncinate processes, that overlap the next rib and stiffen the cage.

layers.basics: The ribs form a stiff cage round the lungs, heart and liver. Each has a little backward hook, the uncinate process, that overlaps the next rib. Only birds have bony hooks of this kind.
layers.deeper: The processes brace the rib cage, anchor muscles of the shoulder blade, and help breathing. In a house sparrow, uncinate processes lie on ribs 14 to 18.
layers.expert: The model draws five pairs of ribs; the real count varies.

facts: bony in birds only (crocodiles have cartilage) (Wikipedia)

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Uncinate processes
summary: Little bony hooks on the ribs.

layers.basics: See the Ribs card: each rib has one that overlaps the next rib.
layers.deeper: Birds only.
layers.expert: Drawn as short rods.

title: Pelvis
summary: The hip bones are fused to the lower back; the joint for the leg is in the middle of the side.

layers.basics: The three hip bones (ilium, ischium, pubis) are fused to the synsacrum. The socket for the thigh bone is in the middle.
layers.deeper: In humans the hip bones form a bowl closed in front.
layers.expert: Drawn as plates.

title: Humerus: the upper arm
summary: The upper arm bone of the wing, the same bone as in your upper arm.

layers.basics: The humerus runs from the shoulder to the elbow. In the folded wing it lies back along the body. It is the bone you feel in your upper arm; a bird's is hollow and light.
layers.deeper: It is one of the bones that may be air-filled. The tendon of the upstroke muscle ends on its upper end.
layers.expert: Drawn as a rod with bulbous ends.

title: Radius and ulna
summary: The two forearm bones, as in your forearm; the ulna carries the secondary flight feathers.

layers.basics: The forearm has two bones, the radius and the ulna, as yours does. The secondary feathers are attached to the ulna.
layers.deeper: The ulna is thicker than the radius.
layers.expert: Drawn as two thin rods.

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Ulna
summary: The thicker forearm bone, with the secondary feathers attached.

layers.basics: See the Radius and ulna card.
layers.deeper: The secondaries are attached to the ulna; the tertials to the tissue at the elbow.
layers.expert: Drawn as a rod.

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Fused hand bone (carpometacarpus)
summary: The wrist and palm bones are fused into one hand bone that carries the primary flight feathers.

layers.basics: In your hand the wrist has eight small bones and the palm has five. In a bird the wrist bones and palm bones are fused into one, the carpometacarpus. It carries the primary feathers and is the part of the wing that makes the main thrust.
layers.deeper: The fused hand gives a rigid support to the long feathers.
layers.expert: Drawn as a rod.

title: Finger bones and the alular digit
summary: Only three fingers remain; the "thumb" carries the alula.

layers.basics: A bird's hand has three digits. The short thumb carries the alula; the longest finger holds the outer primaries. Which digits of the original five these are is debated.
layers.deeper: Fossils suggest digits I-II-III; the embryo suggests II-III-IV.
layers.expert: Drawn as two thin rods and a stub.

open_questions: Which digits does the bird hand keep: I-II-III (fossils) or II-III-IV (embryos)?

title: Leg bones: femur, tibiotarsus, fibula, tarsometatarsus
summary: The thigh bone lies inside the body; the long shin bone and the foot bone make the thin legs.

layers.basics: Inside the belly feathers the thigh bone (femur) runs forward to the knee. Below the knee is the shin bone, the tibiotarsus, with a thin splint (the fibula). The next long bone is the foot bone, the tarsometatarsus, which stands up from the ground and makes what looks like a lower leg.
layers.deeper: The joint between the tibiotarsus and the tarsometatarsus is the ankle.
layers.expert: Drawn as rods.

facts: femur, tibia and fibula; the foot bones are fused

title: Thigh bone (femur)
summary: The thigh bone, inside the belly feathers.

layers.basics: See the Leg bones card for how the leg bones fit together.
layers.deeper: It is part of the leg: femur, tibiotarsus, fibula, tarsometatarsus.
layers.expert: Drawn as a rod.

title: Shin bone (tibiotarsus)
summary: The long shin bone.

layers.basics: See the Leg bones card for how the leg bones fit together.
layers.deeper: It is part of the leg: femur, tibiotarsus, fibula, tarsometatarsus.
layers.expert: Drawn as a rod.

title: Fibula
summary: A thin splint beside the shin bone.

layers.basics: See the Leg bones card for how the leg bones fit together.
layers.deeper: It is part of the leg: femur, tibiotarsus, fibula, tarsometatarsus.
layers.expert: Drawn as a rod.

title: Foot bone (tarsometatarsus)
summary: The long, upright foot bone.

layers.basics: See the Leg bones card for how the leg bones fit together.
layers.deeper: It is part of the leg: femur, tibiotarsus, fibula, tarsometatarsus.
layers.expert: Drawn as a rod.

title: Toe bones
summary: The toes have 3, 4 and 5 bones in the three front toes and 2 in the hind toe.

layers.basics: Each toe is a chain of small bones. In a perching bird the three front toes have 3, 4 and 5 bones and the hind toe has two.
layers.deeper: The last bone carries the claw.
layers.expert: Drawn as short rods end to end.

title: Heart
summary: A four-chambered heart, large and fast for the bird's size, that pumps blood to the flight muscles.

layers.basics: The heart has four chambers: two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it. The right side sends blood to the lungs; the left side sends it round the body. The two sides do not mix, so the muscles get blood full of oxygen. A bird's heart has to supply the most energy-hungry muscles of any animal, so it is large and beats very fast. Use "Cut open: the heart" to see the chambers.
layers.deeper: Oxygen-poor blood comes into the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle, goes to the lungs, returns to the left atrium and is pumped by the left ventricle round the body. The wall of the left ventricle is the thickest. The model's heart pulses as an illustration, with no real rate.
layers.expert: A small songbird's heart beats several hundred times a minute: a similar-sized tropical songbird in the wild ranged from 260 to 824 beats a minute, mean 492 (Steiger et al. 2009). Relative heart size is a good indicator of how much a bird or mammal can sustain locomotion for a long time.

ext.title: Steiger et al. 2009: Heart-rate telemetry of a small tropical bird, the spotted antbird (Physiol. Biochem. Zool.)

title: Left ventricle
summary: The thick-walled chamber that pumps oxygen-rich blood round the whole body.

layers.basics: The left ventricle receives blood that has been to the lungs and pumps it to the body through the main artery (the aorta). Its wall is the thickest in the heart.
layers.deeper: The main artery (the aorta) leaves the heart and curves to the body.
layers.expert: The cavity is drawn as an ellipsoid inside the heart muscle.

title: Right ventricle
summary: The chamber that pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.

layers.basics: The right ventricle wraps round part of the left one. It sends blood to the lungs for oxygen.
layers.deeper: Its wall is thinner than that of the left ventricle.
layers.expert: A crescent in the model.

title: Left atrium
summary: The small chamber that receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.

layers.basics: Blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium and flows on to the left ventricle.
layers.deeper: The atria are thin-walled receiving chambers.
layers.expert: Drawn as a small ellipsoid.

title: Right atrium
summary: The small chamber that receives oxygen-poor blood from the body.

layers.basics: Blood from the body returns to the right atrium and flows on to the right ventricle.
layers.deeper: The atria are thin-walled receiving chambers.
layers.expert: Drawn as a small ellipsoid.

title: Liver
summary: The liver, a large two-lobed organ behind the heart.

layers.basics: The liver is the biggest gland of the body. It makes bile, which helps digest fat, stores sugar and cleans the blood. In a bird it has two lobes, the right slightly bigger.
layers.deeper: It lies just behind the heart, in front of the stomach.
layers.expert: Drawn as two lobes.

title: Gullet (oesophagus), and the crop question
summary: The tube from the throat to the stomach. Some birds have a crop, a pouch for storing food; the model draws none.

layers.basics: Food goes from the throat to the stomach down the gullet, behind the windpipe. Many birds have a crop on the way down, an enlarged part of the gullet where food is stored and softened; not all birds have one (owls do not). The model draws the robin's gullet as a tube with only a gentle widening low in the neck, and no crop.
layers.deeper: A crop is "essentially an enlarged part of the oesophagus". Descriptions of songbirds often mention a slight widening of the lower gullet rather than a true crop.
layers.expert: Descriptions of songbird anatomy differ on whether a true crop is present; the model draws a small widening only.

facts: absent in some birds (owls); robin drawn without a true crop
open_questions: Does the robin have a true crop or only a small widening of the lower gullet?

title: Proventriculus: the glandular stomach
summary: The first of the bird's two stomachs: it adds acid and enzymes.

layers.basics: A bird's stomach has two parts. The first, the proventriculus, makes digestive juices. The food then goes to the muscular second part, the gizzard.
layers.deeper: Acid, mucus and the enzyme pepsin are made here.
layers.expert: Drawn as a small oval.

title: Gizzard: the muscular stomach
summary: The gizzard is the muscle that grinds food, doing the work of teeth.

layers.basics: Birds have no teeth; they grind food in the gizzard, a thick-walled muscular stomach. Some birds swallow grit to help.
layers.deeper: The gizzard is made of four muscular bands. Gizzard stones are shared with the dinosaurs birds came from.
layers.expert: Drawn as a rounded disc.

title: Spleen
summary: A small dark organ beside the stomach that handles blood and immune cells.

layers.basics: The spleen is a small round organ near the stomach. It filters the blood and stores immune cells.
layers.deeper: It is part of the immune system.
layers.expert: Drawn as a small ball.

title: Pancreas
summary: A thin gland that lies in the loop of the first part of the gut and makes digestive enzymes and hormones.

layers.basics: The pancreas makes enzymes that go into the gut and hormones such as insulin and glucagon. It lies in the loop of the gut.
layers.deeper: Compared with mammals birds have a lower insulin-to-glucagon ratio, and fasting blood sugar is 150 to 300 % higher.
layers.expert: Drawn as a thin rod.

title: Intestines and rectum
summary: The gut tube coils in the belly and ends in a short rectum and the cloaca.

layers.basics: Food passes from the gizzard along the small intestine, where it is digested and absorbed, to a short rectum. A bird's gut is short, which keeps its weight down.
layers.deeper: The first part makes a loop around the pancreas.
layers.expert: Drawn as a coiled tube; the real gut is more folded.

title: Rectum
summary: The last short piece of the gut.

layers.basics: See the Intestines card.
layers.deeper: It opens into the cloaca.
layers.expert: Drawn as a short tube.

title: Cloaca: one opening for everything
summary: Gut, kidneys and reproductive organs all open into one chamber, the cloaca.

layers.basics: A bird has one exit for droppings, urine and eggs or sperm. A bird's waste nitrogen leaves as uric acid, a white paste, together with the faeces.
layers.deeper: The bursa of Fabricius, an organ that makes some immune cells in young birds, is a pouch attached to the top of the cloaca.
layers.expert: Drawn as a small chamber.

title: Kidneys
summary: Two kidneys, in hollows under the fused lower back, that clean the blood and make uric acid.

layers.basics: The kidneys filter waste from the blood. In a bird each kidney has three lobes and lies in a hollow of the pelvis. Birds make uric acid, which needs little water.
layers.deeper: There is no bladder; urine goes to the cloaca.
layers.expert: Drawn as three lobes on each side.

title: Eyeballs
summary: The two eyeballs, each about 8 mm across in the model, set in sockets at the sides of the skull.

layers.basics: The eyeballs fill a large part of the head. Each eye has a cornea, a lens and a retina; a bird's retina has a pleated fold, the pecten. Use "Cut open: the eye" to look inside one.
layers.deeper: A ring of small bones in the front of the eye supports its shape.
layers.expert: The size is drawn by eye from the proportions of a robin's head; it is not measured.

title: Lungs
summary: The lungs are small, spongy and fixed against the ribs; they do not expand, the air sacs move the air.

layers.basics: A bird's lungs are small and firm, pressed against the back of the rib cage. They do not swell and shrink: the air sacs do the pumping. Gas exchange takes place in tiny tubes, the parabronchi, with a one-way flow of air.
layers.deeper: See the card on how a robin breathes.
layers.expert: The lung is drawn as a wedge on each side of the spine.

ext.title: Airflow through the avian respiratory system, a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds (open-access paper)

title: Air sacs
summary: Thin-walled air sacs fill much of the body and work as bellows, so that air flows through the lung in one direction.

layers.basics: Air sacs are thin bags that sit among the organs and even in some bones. They hold air and act as bellows. Fresh air goes first into the rear sacs, then through the lungs, then to the front sacs and out. Nine are usual in birds; the model draws one in the front of the chest (interclavicular), a pair in the neck base (cervical), two pairs in the chest (anterior and posterior thoracic) and a pair in the belly (abdominal).
layers.deeper: The posterior sacs receive most of the inhaled air; the anterior sacs empty through the windpipe.
layers.expert: Wikipedia says passerines have seven sacs; descriptions differ, and the model draws the usual nine.

open_questions: How many air sacs a robin has: descriptions differ (nine in the textbook pattern, seven for passerines in one source).

ext.title: Airflow through the avian respiratory system, a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds (open-access paper)

layers.deeper: The sacs work as bellows.

summary: A pair of air sacs in the front of the chest.

layers.basics: This is one of the bird's air sacs. The front group (interclavicular, anterior thoracic, cervical) empty through the windpipe; the rear group (posterior thoracic and abdominal) receive most inhaled air. See the Air sacs card.
layers.deeper: The sacs work as bellows.

summary: A pair of air sacs in the rear of the chest.

layers.basics: This is one of the bird's air sacs. The front group (interclavicular, anterior thoracic, cervical) empty through the windpipe; the rear group (posterior thoracic and abdominal) receive most inhaled air. See the Air sacs card.
layers.deeper: The sacs work as bellows.

title: Abdominal air sacs
summary: A pair of large air sacs among the gut.

layers.basics: This is one of the bird's air sacs. The front group (interclavicular, anterior thoracic, cervical) empty through the windpipe; the rear group (posterior thoracic and abdominal) receive most inhaled air. See the Air sacs card.
layers.deeper: The sacs work as bellows.
layers.expert: Drawn as a smooth bag.
