title: Windpipe (trachea)
summary: The windpipe is a tube of rings from the throat to the syrinx, deep in the chest.

layers.basics: The trachea carries air from the throat to the lungs, down the front of the neck. It is held open by rings of cartilage. At its lower end it splits in two at the syrinx, where the sound is made.
layers.deeper: The tracheal rings are mostly complete rings; the bronchi have C-shaped rings.
layers.expert: Drawn as a smooth tube; the cut-open syrinx view shows the rings.

title: Brain
summary: The brain: a smooth, small brain with large optic lobes.

layers.basics: Much of the brain deals with sight: the optic lobes at the sides are large, because vision matters so much to a bird. The cerebellum at the back controls balance and movement.
layers.deeper: A bird's brain is smooth, without the folds of a human brain.
layers.expert: Drawn by eye from a typical songbird brain.

title: Optic lobes
summary: The parts of the brain that receive signals from the eyes.

layers.basics: The optic lobes are two bulges at the sides of the midbrain. They receive the signals from the optic nerves.
layers.deeper: They are large in birds.
layers.expert: Drawn as ellipsoids.

title: Optic nerves
summary: The cables that carry signals from each eye to the brain.

layers.basics: Each optic nerve leaves the back of the eye and runs to the brain.
layers.deeper: The nerve leaves the retina where the pecten stands.
layers.expert: Drawn as thin cables.

title: Spinal cord
summary: The spinal cord runs from the brain through the vertebrae to the tail.

layers.basics: The spinal cord carries signals between the brain and the body. It runs in a canal inside the vertebrae.
layers.deeper: Nerves leave it between the vertebrae to the wings, the legs and the muscles.
layers.expert: Drawn as a tube.

title: Nerves of the wing and the leg, and the vagus
summary: Nerves branch from the spinal cord to the wings and legs; the vagus nerves run between the brain and the heart and gut.

layers.basics: The nerves of the wing come from a bundle (the brachial plexus) near the shoulder. The big nerve of the leg is the sciatic nerve. The vagus nerves run along the neck to the heart, lungs and gut.
layers.deeper: These nerves have the same names as those in a human.
layers.expert: Drawn as thin cables.

title: Wing nerves (brachial plexus)
summary: See the card on the nerves of the wing and the leg.

layers.basics: The nerves of the wing and the leg branch from the spinal cord; the vagus nerves run along the neck.
layers.deeper: Same names as in a human.
layers.expert: Drawn as thin cables.

title: Leg nerve (sciatic)
summary: See the card on the nerves of the wing and the leg.

layers.basics: The nerves of the wing and the leg branch from the spinal cord; the vagus nerves run along the neck.
layers.deeper: Same names as in a human.
layers.expert: Drawn as thin cables.

title: Vagus nerves
summary: See the card on the nerves of the wing and the leg.

layers.basics: The nerves of the wing and the leg branch from the spinal cord; the vagus nerves run along the neck.
layers.deeper: Same names as in a human.
layers.expert: Drawn as thin cables.

title: Syrinx: where the song is made
summary: The syrinx is the bird's voice box, at the base of the windpipe where it forks, not in the throat.

layers.basics: A bird's throat (the larynx) does not make its song. The sound is made lower down, deep in the chest, in the syrinx. It sits where the windpipe splits to go to the two lungs. Thin membranes vibrate as air passes, and muscles change their tension. The bird can control each side separately.
layers.deeper: In songbirds the syrinx is the tracheobronchial form: the lower trachea and the upper bronchi. The tracheal rings are mostly complete; the bronchial rings are C-shaped, with smooth muscle in the open part. Sound comes from vibration of the membrana tympaniformis and the pessulus.
layers.expert: The syrinx is drawn at true size, a few millimetres wide, and simplified. The model windpipe is about 2 mm across; real dimensions vary between birds.

facts: where the windpipe forks, above the lungs

title: Pessulus
summary: A small bony wedge at the fork of the windpipe, between the two bronchi.

layers.basics: The pessulus stands in the middle of the fork like the point of a Y. In songbirds it is bony. Air flows on both sides of it.
layers.deeper: Sound comes from the vibration of the thin membranes and of the pessulus.
layers.expert: Drawn as a small wedge.

title: Tympaniform membranes
summary: Thin membranes in the wall of each bronchus that vibrate to make the sound.

layers.basics: When air from the lungs flows over them, the membranes vibrate, like the reed of a clarinet or the lips of a trumpeter. Each side has its own.
layers.deeper: In most passerines the membrane that forms part of the first three bronchial rings makes the sound.
layers.expert: Drawn as small discs.

title: Syringeal muscles
summary: Small muscles that tune the syrinx; songbirds control them more finely than any other birds.

layers.basics: Muscles on the outside of each bronchus tighten the membranes and change the pitch. Songbirds have the finest control of these muscles of any bird, which allows their wide range of songs.
layers.deeper: The intrinsic muscles are in the syrinx; the extrinsic muscles, such as the sternotrachealis, run from outside.
layers.expert: Drawn as a band on each bronchus.

title: Rings of the windpipe and bronchi
summary: The rings of cartilage that hold the windpipe open; the bronchi have C-shaped rings.

layers.basics: The trachea is stiffened by rings of cartilage, mostly complete. The bronchi have C-shaped rings with smooth muscle along the open part.
layers.deeper: The spacing changes near the syrinx.
layers.expert: Drawn as 9 rings and 8 C-shaped rings on each bronchus.

title: Bronchus
summary: One of the two tubes that carry air from the syrinx to the lungs.

layers.basics: The bronchi carry air from the fork of the windpipe to each lung.
layers.deeper: The syrinx covers the lowest part of the trachea and the upper bronchi.
layers.expert: Drawn leaving the fork at 40 degrees.

title: Sclera
summary: The tough white outer wall of the eyeball.

layers.basics: The sclera is the strong outer coat of the eye, white in humans, and keeps its shape.
layers.deeper: In birds it carries a ring of small bones round the front.
layers.expert: Drawn as a shell.

title: Scleral ring: small bones in the eye
summary: A ring of small bone plates in the front of the sclera, round the cornea.

layers.basics: In the front of a bird's eye there is a ring of thin bony plates (scleral ossicles) set in the sclera. They support the shape of the eye and give the muscles of focusing something to attach to.
layers.deeper: Most birds have about 12 to 18 plates in each ring; 14 is most common.
layers.expert: Drawn as a single ring.

title: Cornea
summary: The clear front window of the eye that does most of the focusing.

layers.basics: The cornea is the transparent front of the eye. It bends the light entering the eye.
layers.deeper: In life the cornea is much thinner than drawn.
layers.expert: The shell is exaggerated for visibility.

title: Iris and pupil
summary: The coloured ring that sets the size of the pupil.

layers.basics: The iris is a ring of muscle round the pupil, the opening for light. A robin's eye looks black.
layers.deeper: The iris adjusts the amount of light.
layers.expert: Drawn as a flat ring.

title: Lens
summary: The lens focuses light on the retina.

layers.basics: The lens sits behind the pupil. Muscles round it change its shape to focus on near and far.
layers.deeper: In birds the muscles that change the shape of the lens attach to the ring of small bones.
layers.expert: Drawn as an ellipsoid.

title: Vitreous body
summary: The clear jelly that fills the eyeball behind the lens.

layers.basics: The vitreous fills most of the eye and holds the retina in place. Light passes through it.
layers.deeper: The pecten reaches into it.
layers.expert: Drawn as a translucent sphere.

title: Choroid
summary: A dark, blood-rich layer behind the retina.

layers.basics: The choroid lies between the retina and the sclera. It is dark, which stops light bouncing around inside the eye, and it holds the blood vessels that feed the outer retina.
layers.deeper: Birds' retinas have almost no blood vessels of their own, so they rely on the choroid and the pecten.
layers.expert: Drawn as a thin dark shell.

title: Retina
summary: The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye; click to look inside it.

layers.basics: The retina is the screen at the back of the eye. It is made of cells that respond to light and pass signals along the optic nerve. Use the button to look inside it.
layers.deeper: A bird's retina is largely free of blood vessels.
layers.expert: See the retina scene for the cells.

facts: largely absent; fed by the choroid and the pecten (Wikipedia)

title: Pecten: the pleated fold in the eye
summary: The pecten is a pleated, blood-rich fold that stands out from the retina into the jelly, found only in birds.

layers.basics: In birds the retina has few blood vessels of its own. A fold of tissue, the pecten (Latin for "comb of the eye"), projects from where the optic nerve enters the eye into the vitreous. It brings blood to feed the retina.
layers.deeper: The pecten has blood vessels, dark pigment cells and supporting tissue, and no muscle or nerve fibres. The pleated type is the commonest and has 5 to 30 pleats. The leading idea is that it nourishes the retina and keeps the vitreous healthy; when the eye makes quick movements the pecten oscillates and stirs the jelly.
layers.expert: The model draws seven pleats.

open_questions: What is the main job of the pecten: feeding the retina, controlling the vitreous pH, absorbing stray light, or all of them?

title: Optic nerve
summary: The cable of nerve fibres from the retina to the brain.

layers.basics: The optic nerve leaves the back of the eye where the pecten stands and runs to the brain.
layers.deeper: It carries the signals of all the retina's ganglion cells.
layers.expert: Drawn as a cable.

title: Inside a feather
summary: A flight feather is a tree: a shaft, side branches (barbs), twigs (barbules) and tiny hooks that zip the vane together.

layers.basics: Look closely at a feather and you find a branching structure. From the central shaft (the rachis) the side branches (barbs) grow out in a row, and from each barb grow even finer twigs, the barbules. The barbules of neighbouring barbs overlap, and tiny hooks hold them together, so the vane is a smooth sheet that air cannot go through. If you pull it apart, the hooks re-engage when you stroke it back, which is what a bird does when it preens.
layers.deeper: The barbules on a flight feather of species from a hummingbird to a condor are spaced only 8 to 16 micrometres apart. The shaft is made of bundles of 3-nanometre keratin filaments embedded in an amorphous keratin matrix.
layers.expert: Sizes drawn in the scene: only the barbule spacing (8 to 16 µm) is a published measurement; the barb and barbule lengths and thicknesses, and the number of hooks, are illustrative.

facts: 3 nm diameter, in the shaft's cortex

ext.title: The feather's multi-functional structure across nano to macro scales inspires hierarchical design (J. R. Soc. Interface 22(225), 2025)

title: Barb
summary: A barb is one of the side branches of a feather's shaft; a row of them makes the vane.

layers.basics: Each barb is a thin rod that grows from the shaft at an angle. A feather vane has hundreds of them side by side.
layers.deeper: Along each barb, barbules branch to both sides.
layers.expert: The lengths and thicknesses drawn are illustrative.

facts: branch of the rachis, bears barbules

title: Barbule: the hooked twigs
summary: The barbules are the fine twigs of the barbs; the hooks of one barbule catch the next.

layers.basics: Each barb carries a row of barbules on each side. The barbules that face the tip of the feather have little hooks; those that face the base have a ridge where the hooks catch. The result is a zip. A barbule is a few micrometres thick and made of dead cells full of keratin. Use the button to see the molecule that links the keratin together.
layers.deeper: Neighbouring barbules sit 8 to 16 micrometres apart.
layers.expert: Each barbule is a chain of dead, keratin-filled cells; the keratin is held together by sulfur bridges.

ext.title: The feather's multi-functional structure across nano to macro scales inspires hierarchical design (J. R. Soc. Interface 22(225), 2025)

title: Hooklets (barbicels)
summary: The tiny hooks on the barbules that grip the next barbule like the loops of a zip.

layers.basics: At the end of a barbule are minute hooks, barbicels, that catch on the ridge of the next barbule. Down feathers lack them, so their barbules float free.
layers.deeper: This is what turns a loose set of branches into a continuous vane.
layers.expert: The hooklets are drawn illustratively: their size and number are not measured.

title: Pigment granules
summary: Brown and black feather colour comes from granules of melanin inside the barbs.

layers.basics: Colour in a feather is mostly made by pigment. The brown of a robin's back is melanin, in small granules inside the barbs and barbules. Use the button to see a molecule on the way to melanin.
layers.deeper: Melanin is made from the amino acid tyrosine through L-DOPA. Whether the orange of the breast is a type of melanin, phaeomelanin, or a carotenoid is not settled.
layers.expert: The granule size and number drawn are illustrative.

title: Inside the flight muscle
summary: The flight muscle is a bundle of long fibres, packed with energy-making mitochondria and fed by many fine blood vessels.

layers.basics: A muscle is made of long cells called fibres. In a flight muscle each fibre is packed with mitochondria, the parts of the cell that burn fuel with oxygen to make the energy molecule ATP. Between the fibres run fine blood vessels. Click a mitochondrion and press the button to see ATP.
layers.deeper: The fibres contract by filaments sliding past each other. The energy comes from ATP, made in the mitochondria and used by the motor protein myosin.
layers.expert: Sizes in the scene are illustrative; the numbers of fibres and mitochondria drawn are for clarity.

title: Muscle fibre
summary: A flight muscle fibre is one long cell, many times longer than it is wide.

layers.basics: Each fibre is a single long cell with many nuclei, filled with bundles of contracting filaments. It is surrounded by capillaries.
layers.deeper: Contraction comes from the sliding of thick and thin filaments.
layers.expert: The fibre drawn is a tube; real fibres are more varied in size.

title: Mitochondria
summary: Mitochondria make most of the muscle's ATP by burning fuel with oxygen.

layers.basics: Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell. Flight uses a lot of energy, so flight muscle is packed with them. They make the energy molecule ATP.
layers.deeper: Oxidative phosphorylation across their inner membrane makes most of the ATP.
layers.expert: Their size and number in the scene are illustrative.

title: Inside a hollow bone
summary: A hollow bone is a thin wall of dense bone round an air-filled space braced by struts.

layers.basics: A cut across a hollow bird bone shows a thin ring of hard bone round an empty (air-filled) space, crossed by thin struts like those in a bridge. The wall is made of bone cells in a framework of protein and mineral.
layers.deeper: Bone cells (osteocytes) live in tiny holes in the wall and keep it alive. The struts stiffen the tube against bending and crushing.
layers.expert: Sizes in the scene are illustrative.

title: Wall of compact bone
summary: The thin, dense wall of a hollow bone.

layers.basics: The wall is dense bone that carries most of the load. Because it is far from the centre of the tube, it makes the tube stiff for little weight.
layers.deeper: Bone is a composite of mineral and protein fibres.
layers.expert: The thickness is illustrative.

title: Strut (trabecula)
summary: Thin struts crossing the hollow of a bone, like the braces in a bridge.

layers.basics: Thin rods of bone cross the hollow space inside many bird bones. They brace the wall against bending and buckling.
layers.deeper: Their arrangement follows the loads on the bone.
layers.expert: Drawn as a random set of thin rods.

title: Bone cell (osteocyte)
summary: The living cell inside a bone, in a tiny pocket of the hard wall.

layers.basics: Osteocytes are the long-lived cells of bone. Each sits in a small space and reaches out to its neighbours with fine arms. Use the button to look inside a cell.
layers.deeper: They sense strain and direct the repair of bone.
layers.expert: Drawn as small ovals; the size is illustrative.

title: Inside the retina
summary: The retina is a screen of light-sensing cells; a protein called cryptochrome is one candidate for a magnetic sensor.

layers.basics: Light entering the eye falls on the retina, which is made of layers of cells. The light-sensing cells, the photoreceptors, hold the molecule retinal, which changes shape when it catches a photon. Some of the retina's proteins, the cryptochromes, may help the robin sense Earth's magnetic field; that is an unproven idea.
layers.deeper: The photoreceptors send signals through other retinal neurons to the optic nerve. A bird's retina is largely free of blood vessels; it is fed from the choroid and the pecten.
layers.expert: The scene is a schematic: the cell shapes and sizes are illustrative, and the place of cryptochrome in a particular cell type is not drawn as a measurement.

title: Photoreceptor cell
summary: A photoreceptor catches light with the molecule retinal and turns it into a nerve signal.

layers.basics: Photoreceptors are the retina's light-sensing cells. Their outer part is full of membranes carrying a light-sensitive protein with retinal. A photon changes retinal's shape and starts a chain of events that ends in a nerve signal. Use the button to see retinal.
layers.deeper: Birds have rods for dim light and cones, with several kinds for colour.
layers.expert: Sizes drawn are illustrative.

title: Cryptochrome 4 (a hypothesis for the magnetic sensor)
summary: A light-sensitive protein that carries the molecule FAD; it is a candidate for the robin's magnetic sensor.

layers.basics: Cryptochrome is a protein that holds a flavin molecule (FAD). When light excites the FAD, an electron jumps along a chain of tryptophan units in the protein, leaving a pair of molecules with unpaired electrons. Earth's magnetic field could affect how long such a pair lasts. This is a hypothesis for how a robin senses the field, not a proved mechanism. Use the button to see FAD.
layers.deeper: In the laboratory, robin cryptochrome 4 shows a four-step electron transfer and long-lived radical pairs. Whether it works as the compass in the bird is not shown.
layers.expert: See the compass card for the evidence and what is missing.

title: Bird
summary: A bird is a feathered animal descended from theropod dinosaurs; the park's bird is a European robin, standing on the boulder.

layers.basics: Birds are the living descendants of feathered dinosaurs. Most fly, with wings, hollow bones, a keeled breastbone and a lung that works with air sacs; some, such as ostriches, do not. The bird in this park is a European robin, standing on the boulder. Click it for its card, or use "Show where it is" to fly to it.
layers.deeper: Birds are theropod dinosaurs, warm-blooded, with feathers, a four-chambered heart and a lung in which air flows in one direction. Zoom in on the robin to see all of that, down to the molecules of its feathers and muscles.
layers.expert: The old cartoon birds are gone; the robin is a data model built to true size. The park is a simplified scene, not a scan of a real place.
